p.title: Complex Contagion Influence Maximization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach

ext.title: Complex Contagion Influence Maximization (RL4CCIM)
ext.venue: IJCAI-23 (Proceedings of the Thirty-Second International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence), pp. 5531-5540. Metadata hint had blank venue, year and DOI; the venue and year are taken from the running header in the text.
ext.document_type: Conference paper (IJCAI-23 proceedings, algorithmic/ML benchmark study)
ext.coverage: Full extracted text read in all chunks (1,329 lines, about 57k chars): title, abstract, introduction, related work, problem formulation, RL4CCIM method, experiments, ablation, limitation, conclusion, references (printed pp. 5531-5540). Appendices A-E (proofs, hyperparameters, network descriptions, MIP formulation, India seed comparison) are cited in the text but are not in the extracted file, so they are not covered. Annotations: all 74 items read (67 Highlight, 6 Ink, 1 FreeText). Only the FreeText item carries note text; it is stored truncated mid-word ("as varia"). Page numbers below are PDF page indices as used in the annotation file (printed journal page = PDF page + 5530). Lobbying, elections, legislators, text measurement, and turnout/persuasion are not discussed in the text; the closest topics are social-network seeding, budget-constrained target selection, and social reinforcement in adoption.
ext.research_question: Can reinforcement learning be used to solve complex contagion influence maximization (CCIM): choosing a fixed budget of seed nodes when cascade probability rises with the number of already-activated neighbors, so the objective is non-submodular? (Sec. 1, PDF p2)
ext.theory: Influence cascades are modeled as independent cascade (IC) or linear threshold (LT), both submodular, so greedy seeding has guarantees (Kempe et al. 2003). Complex contagion (Centola and Macy 2007) makes adoption probability jump when enough neighbors are active (S-shaped diffusion, Backstrom et al. 2006), which breaks submodularity and creates complementarities among seeds. The K-complex model (Eq. 1) sets activation probability to p0 when at least K neighbors are active and p1 otherwise, with 0 <= p1 << p0 <= 1. The authors frame seed selection as an MDP where each time step adds one seed, and reward is the marginal spread gain; sparse rewards are the central obstacle.
ext.data: Nine networks; no observation period is stated in the extracted text, and the study simulates cascades rather than using observed adoption data. Unit: network nodes (individuals in the social networks). Five small social networks collected from homeless youth shelters in Los Angeles: CHANGE, DC, DOSIM, MFP, SPY. Four public networks: Football (Girvan and Newman 2002), Polbooks (Rossi and Ahmed 2015), India (Banerjee et al. 2013), Exhibition (Isella et al. 2011). Node counts appear in the text only for India (202 nodes) and SPY (67 nodes); other sizes are in Appendix C, which is not in the extract. Basic setting: p0=1, p1=0 (deterministic), seed budget T=8 (T=12 for Exhibition), threshold K=3 for CHANGE-SPY, K=4 for Football, Polbooks, India, K=6 for Exhibition.
ext.method: Algorithmic benchmark, no causal design. Proposed RL4CCIM builds on the RL4IM/S2V line (Khalil et al. 2017; Chen et al. 2021) and uses Double-DQN (Van Hasselt et al. 2016) with four changes: (1) Solution filtering: candidate set A is the union of neighborhoods of every node with at least K neighbors; exploration samples from A with probability eps*eps', eps' annealed from 0.99 to 0 (Alg. 1 lines 3-5, 9; Thm 3). (2) Reward-based prioritized experience replay with priority (|delta| + beta*r + eps)^alpha (Eq. 5). (3) Reward shaping r' = r + omega*r_global, where r_global is the action's marginal contribution given all seeds chosen in the episode (Eqs. 6-7); this needs a full simulation before per-step rewards are assigned. (4) Graph attention network (GAT) replaces S2V as the graph encoder. Baselines: Random+ (seeds drawn from A, 50 runs averaged), Greedy (Kempe et al. 2003), DPIM (Angell and Schoenebeck 2017; authors' own reimplementation because code is not public), RL4IM (Chen et al. 2021), and OPT from a Gurobi mixed-integer program on small networks only (12-hour limit, exceeded from SPY onward per text). RL methods: 15 runs, best model chosen by validation every 20 training steps. Training finishes within 2 hours. Hyperparameters are in Appendix B (not in extract).
ext.scope: Algorithmic influence maximization on nine small to medium social and contact networks, with simulated K-complex cascades. Population: no human subjects; the five shelter networks come from LA homeless youth shelters, cited to Wilder et al. 2021 for the HIV-prevention setting. Institutions: a multi-institution computer science and AI group (William and Mary, CMU, NTU, USC, Harvard). Era: IJCAI-23, 2023. The paper says training time and scalability are not the focus, so all experiments use small networks. Nothing here addresses lobbying, elections, legislators, text measurement, or turnout.

key_findings.finding: Complex contagion influence maximization is non-submodular (Theorem 1) and K-complex contagion IM is NP-hard (Theorem 2), shown by reduction from IC when K=1. Proofs are in Appendix A, which is not in the extract.
key_findings.numbers: None reported beyond the K=1 reduction

key_findings.finding: Reward sparseness has two sources: effective-solution sparseness (few seed sets activate anyone) and credit sparseness (rewards stay flat until several seeds are chosen).
key_findings.location: Sec. 1 PDF p2; Sec. 5.1 PDF p4 (printed 5534)
key_findings.numbers: Toy network (Fig. 2, 8 nodes, p0=1, p1=0, K=3, T=4): 17 of C(8,4)=70 four-seed sets are effective, 24.3%. Seed sequence {1,2,3,5} gives per-step rewards 1,1,1,2.

key_findings.finding: Solution filtering keeps only nodes that could be part of an effective solution (neighborhoods of nodes with at least K neighbors). Theorem 3 says no effective solution is excluded.
key_findings.numbers: Toy example: feasible sets shrink from 70 to 15, which is 21.4% of the original space. The text also says 24.2% of nodes (not sets) have non-zero reward, which conflicts with 24.3% in Sec. 5.1.

key_findings.finding: In the deterministic basic setting, RL4CCIM has the highest normalized influence on all nine networks, by the authors' account, with some ties.
key_findings.numbers: Football 1.0 (RL4IM 0.513, DPIM 0.3913, Greedy 0.3217); Polbooks 0.819 (RL4IM 0.7429, DPIM 0.6762); India 0.5347 (DPIM 0.3911, RL4IM 0.3465, Greedy 0.0396); Exhibition 0.5585 (DPIM 0.5537, RL4IM 0.5439, Greedy 0.0293); CHANGE 0.283, tied with DPIM and RL4IM (Greedy 0.1509).

key_findings.finding: On small networks where exact MIP gives a value, RL4CCIM matches the optimum on DC and DOSIM and is slightly below it elsewhere.
key_findings.numbers: DC 0.4634 = OPT; DOSIM 0.375 = OPT; CHANGE 0.283 vs OPT 0.3019 (about 6.3% below, derived); MFP 0.3472 vs 0.375 (about 7.4% below, derived); SPY 0.5075 vs 0.5522 (about 8.1% below, derived).

key_findings.finding: Greedy performs very poorly on some networks. The authors say it finds no effective solution on India (202 nodes).
key_findings.location: Sec. 6.1 PDF p7; seed comparison in Appendix E (not in extract)
key_findings.numbers: Greedy 0.0396 on India vs RL4CCIM 0.5347; Random+ 0.0498 on India; Greedy and Random+ both 0.0293 on Exhibition.

key_findings.finding: RL4IM and DPIM are unstable across networks. The authors attribute DPIM's gaps to its hierarchy assumption and RL4IM's to effective-solution sparseness that grows with solution-space size. Both explanations are stated as hypotheses.
key_findings.numbers: RL4IM Football 0.513 vs 1.0; DPIM Football 0.3913 and India 0.3911 vs RL4CCIM 1.0 and 0.5347.

key_findings.finding: RL4CCIM beats all baselines across a sensitivity sweep of propagation probability, budget and threshold on India, Football and Polbooks. Greedy jumps on India when T rises from 12 to 14 and K falls from 4 to 3, which the authors attribute to a larger share of effective solutions.
key_findings.numbers: p1 in {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1}; T in {6, 8, 10, 12, 14}; K in {2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (K=5 used for Football T-sweep). Fig. 4 plotted values are not in the extracted text.

key_findings.finding: Ablation on India: removing each component lowers normalized influence, and removing all of them (which equals RL4IM) lowers it most.
key_findings.numbers: Drops: w/o solution filtering 10.2%; w/o PER 4.6%; w/o reward shaping 9.3%; w/o GAT 21.3%; w/o all components 35.2%.

key_findings.finding: Scalability is the main limitation: simulation time for complex contagion is the top bottleneck, followed by Q-network gradient cost on large graphs. Pruning is suggested as a remedy.
key_findings.numbers: All experiments use small networks; RL training finishes within 2 hours (Sec. 6 PDF p6).

key_findings.finding: Solution filtering alone and PER alone each contribute a measurable share of the gain, and the authors judge the combined components necessary.
key_findings.numbers: See ablation drops above (10.2% and 4.6% respectively).

limitations: Scalability: complex-contagion simulation cost and Q-network training cost limit the method to small networks; the authors present pruning as an unexplored fix (PDF p8).
The paper says training time and scalability are not its focus; all experiments run on small networks (PDF p6).

The DPIM baseline is the authors' own reimplementation (original code not public), using a Jaccard-similarity hierarchical decomposition (PDF p6). Results for this baseline therefore depend on that implementation.

The MIP optimum was reported as exceeding the 12-hour limit starting at SPY (67 nodes), yet Table 1 gives an OPT value for SPY (0.5522). This conflict is not explained in the text and should be checked.
Table 1 is limited to the deterministic setting (p1=0, p0=1). Stochastic propagation appears only in Fig. 4, and its plotted values are not in the extracted text.
K and T were chosen by the authors per network to keep spread neither too sparse nor too dense (PDF p7), so the reported comparisons depend on those choices.
Only nine networks are tested, and the paper does not test transfer to new networks, which it lists as future work (Conclusion, PDF p8).

Node heterogeneity is absent: Eq. 1 applies one threshold K and one pair (p0, p1) to every node, with no node-level status or rank term. Paul's margin note asks about high-ranking members, and the text does not address that question.

Internal inconsistencies: the 24.3% vs 24.2% figure for effective solutions (Sec. 5.1 vs 5.3, where 24.2% is described as a share of nodes, not solutions); and the ablation text says 'removing the 3 components altogether' while listing four components and an all-removed variant (Sec. 6.3).
The definition of 'normalized influence' used as the outcome in Table 1 and Figs. 4-5 is not given in the extracted text.
The explanations for DPIM and RL4IM instability are the authors' hypotheses and were not tested in the paper (PDF p7).
Appendices A-E (proofs, hyperparameter ranges, network descriptions, MIP formulation, seed comparison) were not in the extract, so claims that depend on them cannot be checked here.
The paper tests simulated cascades only; it does not validate the K-complex model against field adoption data, though it cites Centola 2010 and Romero et al. 2011 as empirical support.
measures: Normalized influence of the seed set under the K-complex cascade model (Table 1, Figs. 4-5); definition not in extract
Optimality gap versus Gurobi MIP optimum on four small networks (derived gaps listed under findings)
Percent drop in normalized influence in the ablation on India
Runs: Random+ 50 averaged, RL methods 15 with validation every 20 steps, Greedy and DPIM 20 averaged in stochastic settings
Sensitivity over propagation probability p1, budget T and threshold K
ext.identification: Not a causal design. The study is an algorithmic benchmark: a fixed set of networks and a simulated cascade model, with no treatment or outcome data. Comparisons use the deterministic basic setting (p1=0, p0=1) to remove simulation noise, then sensitivity sweeps over p1, T and K. RL model selection uses a separate validation process every 20 training steps.
references_of_note: Kempe, Kleinberg and Tardos 2003, KDD: foundational influence maximization; greedy with ratio 1-1/e under submodular IC/LT.
Centola and Macy 2007, American Journal of Sociology: complex contagion model, cascade probability rises with number of activated neighbors.
Centola 2010, Science: online network experiment; adoption more likely with social reinforcement from multiple neighbors.
Angell and Schoenebeck 2017, WINE: DPIM, the only prior practical method for non-submodular IM; relies on hierarchical network structure.
Schoenebeck and Tao 2019, ACM TOCT: CCIM is NP-hard to approximate even under simplified network models.
Schoenebeck, Tao and Yu 2020, arXiv:2003.10393: optimal seeding for non-submodular IM on stochastic hierarchical blockmodels.
Banerjee et al. 2013, Science: diffusion of microfinance; source of the India network.
Beaman et al. 2021, American Economic Review: network-theory-based targeting for technology adoption.
Kim et al. 2015, The Lancet: social network targeting to maximize population behavior change (cluster RCT).
Wilder et al. 2021, AAAI: AI-augmented HIV prevention intervention among youth experiencing homelessness; cited as the motivating domain.
Chen et al. 2021, arXiv:2106.07039: RL4IM, the authors' prior RL method for submodular IM and a baseline here.
Manchanda et al. 2020, NeurIPS (GCOMB): RL for budget-constrained graph combinatorial problems; marginal-contribution reward; graph pruning.
Khalil et al. 2017, NeurIPS: RL with graph embeddings (S2V) for combinatorial optimization over graphs.
Kamarthi et al. 2020, AAMAS: influence maximization in unknown networks via learned graph sampling.
Backstrom et al. 2006, KDD; Romero et al. 2011, WWW; Ugander et al. 2012, PNAS: empirical evidence for S-shaped or complex contagion.

paul_entries.text:
**Chen, H., Wilder, B., Qiu, W., An, B., Rice, E., & Tambe, M. (2023).** *Complex Contagion Influence Maximization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach.* IJCAI '23, 5531–5540. https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2023/614 (RL4CCIM)

The clearest published validation of the master/subordinate split, and the most important paper in this section for Melange's theory. Complex contagion — where a node's adoption probability rises sharply with the *number* of already-activated neighbors — is **non-submodular**, which breaks the diminishing-returns property that the greedy (1 − 1/e) guarantee depends on. The authors give the first RL approach to the problem and identify reward sparseness as the core obstacle, addressing it with a reward-shaping component (marginal-contribution rewards at episode end) and return-based prioritized experience replay. This is precisely why the outer MDP layer cannot be replaced by iterated greedy. Note the substantive implication: coalition formation in Congress is plausibly a complex contagion (a fence-sitter commits only once enough allies already have), which would place Melange's core problem *outside* the submodular regime and squarely in the RL envelope.
